results.name: distance_gradient_corr
results.description: Correlation between rating and log(1 + distance from target to nearest example) over non-example targets; more negative than null means humans show a steeper numeric-similarity gradient than the model, less negative means a shallower one.
results.code:
# name: distance_gradient_corr
# description: Correlation between rating and log(1 + distance from target to nearest example) over non-example targets; more negative than null means humans show a steeper numeric-similarity gradient than the model, less negative means a shallower one.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",").apply(lambda l: np.array([int(x) for x in l]))
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    dist = np.array([np.min(np.abs(a - x)) for a, x in zip(ex.values, t)])
    m = dist > 0
    x = np.log1p(dist[m]); y = df["rating"].values[m].astype(float)
    if x.std() == 0 or y.std() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.corrcoef(x, y)[0, 1])

results.name: residual_lag1_autocorr
results.description: Lag-1 correlation of response residuals (rating minus its (set,target) cell mean) between consecutive trials of the same session (trial_index increments by 1); observed above null means sequential response perseveration the trial-independent model lacks.
results.code:
# name: residual_lag1_autocorr
# description: Lag-1 correlation of response residuals (rating minus its (set,target) cell mean) between consecutive trials of the same session (trial_index increments by 1); observed above null means sequential response perseveration the trial-independent model lacks.
def test_statistic(df):
    r = df["rating"].values.astype(float)
    cm = df.groupby(["number_set", "target"])["rating"].transform("mean").values
    res = r - cm
    ti = df["trial_index"].values
    ok = np.diff(ti) == 1
    a = res[:-1][ok]; b = res[1:][ok]
    if len(a) < 3 or a.std() == 0 or b.std() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.corrcoef(a, b)[0, 1])

results.name: singleton_nonmember_yes
results.description: Yes-rate to non-example targets after a single-example set; observed above null means people generalize more broadly from one example than the size-principle model (below null: more narrowly).

results.name: early_minus_late_yes
results.description: Yes-rate on trials with trial_index < 90 minus yes-rate on trials with trial_index >= 90; observed above null means people grow more conservative over the session, a drift the stationary model cannot produce.

results.name: far_rule_consistent_yes
results.description: Among multi-example sets with all examples of one parity and span <= 20, yes-rate to same-parity non-example targets >= 25 from the nearest example; observed above null means the model's range restriction over-suppresses far rule members (below null: under-suppresses).
results.code:
# name: far_rule_consistent_yes
# description: Among multi-example sets with all examples of one parity and span <= 20, yes-rate to same-parity non-example targets >= 25 from the nearest example; observed above null means the model's range restriction over-suppresses far rule members (below null: under-suppresses).
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",")
    ex = sets.apply(lambda l: np.array([int(x) for x in l]))
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    n = ex.apply(len).values
    mn = ex.apply(np.min).values; mx = ex.apply(np.max).values
    par = ex.apply(lambda a: int(a[0] % 2) if np.all(a % 2 == a[0] % 2) else -1).values
    dist = np.array([np.min(np.abs(a - x)) for a, x in zip(ex.values, t)])
    mask = (n >= 2) & (par >= 0) & (mx - mn <= 20) & (t % 2 == par) & (dist >= 25)
    if mask.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].values[mask].mean())

results.name: off_parity_within_span_yes
results.description: Among multi-example sets whose examples all share parity, yes-rate to opposite-parity targets lying inside the examples' [min,max] span; observed above null means the model under-weights range/similarity relative to parity rules for in-span targets.
results.code:
# name: off_parity_within_span_yes
# description: Among multi-example sets whose examples all share parity, yes-rate to opposite-parity targets lying inside the examples' [min,max] span; observed above null means the model under-weights range/similarity relative to parity rules for in-span targets.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",").apply(lambda l: np.array([int(x) for x in l]))
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    n = ex.apply(len).values
    mn = ex.apply(np.min).values; mx = ex.apply(np.max).values
    par = ex.apply(lambda a: int(a[0] % 2) if np.all(a % 2 == a[0] % 2) else -1).values
    mask = (n >= 2) & (par >= 0) & (t > mn) & (t < mx) & (t % 2 != par)
    if mask.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].values[mask].mean())

results.name: in_set_target_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate on trials whose target is one of the shown examples; observed below null means people miss/lapse on trivially consistent targets that the lapse-free model answers "yes" to almost surely.

results.name: cell_extremity
results.description: Mean over (set,target) cells of |cell yes-rate - 0.5|; observed below null means the model's predictions are over-confident (too close to 0/1) relative to graded human responding.
